WA Archive keeps your WhatsApp history on your own Mac. It pairs with an iPhone over USB, pulls a backup, and turns it into a searchable archive on an encrypted volume you control. Nothing leaves the machine except the check for its own updates.
### Added
- **A model running on this Mac can read the archive, once you allow it.** Settings has a Local AI access pane with a single switch, off until you turn it on. It names the archive it would expose and how much of a message a model may see, and it refuses every client while the app is locked. Nothing reaches the network; the model has to already be on this machine. - **Later acquisitions can copy only what changed.** Keep a retained backup at the end of a run and the next one refreshes it instead of pulling the phone in full. The wizard offers the choice, and it checks there is room for both copies before it starts. A first acquisition is unaffected and still copies the phone in full.
### Fixed
- **The app no longer carries the name of the Mac it was built on.** Every release before this one shipped the build machine's macOS account name inside the app: 677 times in the main program, and once in each of the 31 helper scripts that came with the bundled Python. No password, key, or message content was ever involved, and nothing was sent anywhere. It was a name and a folder layout, in an app whose point is that your messages stay on your machine. Both earlier releases still carry it, because a published download cannot be edited in place. Packaging now checks the finished app for anything of the kind and refuses to release it otherwise.

WA Archive keeps your WhatsApp history on your own Mac. It pairs with an iPhone over USB, pulls a backup, and turns it into a searchable archive on an encrypted volume you control. Nothing leaves the machine except the check for its own updates.
### Installing
Download `WAArchive.dmg` below, open it, and drag WA Archive into your Applications folder. Run it from Applications rather than from the disk image. macOS keeps a downloaded app read-only until you move it, and an update cannot install over a read-only copy.
macOS asks you to confirm the first time you open it. Click Open. It says Apple checked the app and found no malicious software, and you see that once.
The first release lists everything the app does: https://github.com/gokul-noon/WAArchive-dist/releases/tag/v0.1.0-1
### What changed
Nothing in the app. This version exists to prove the update path.
If you are reading this inside WA Archive, it worked. Your copy checked the signed feed, found this version, verified its Ed25519 signature against the key compiled into it, and replaced itself. Every version after this one arrives the same way, so nobody needs to send you a download link again.

First release.
### Added
- **Your WhatsApp history, kept on your own Mac.** WA Archive pairs with an iPhone over USB, pulls a WhatsApp backup, and turns it into a searchable archive on an encrypted volume you control. Nothing leaves the machine, and the app makes no network request outside checking for its own updates. - **Search that works on real messages.** Full-text search covers Latin and non-Latin scripts, emoji, and mixed queries, with sort, keyset paging, and jumps to any date in the middle of a conversation. - **Media alongside the transcript.** Photos, video thumbnails, voice notes converted for playback, and waveform display, with every attachment inline where it was sent. - **Storage you can measure and reclaim.** Retention tooling breaks usage into five categories and deletes what you choose in one confirmation, leaving source backups alone. - **The archive is readable by your own tools.** A local API and an MCP server serve chats, transcripts, search, stats, and media over stdio, and `export` writes the whole archive to NDJSON with a manifest. - **The app updates itself.** Sparkle checks a signed feed, verifies each update with an Ed25519 signature before installing, and shows these notes.
### Security
- Every release is signed with a Developer ID certificate, notarized by Apple, and stapled, so macOS opens it without a warning. Each download publishes a SHA-256 checksum and a provenance record naming the exact commit it was built from.
